text_fidelity_a:
Shure AONIC 215 Wired Sound Isolating Earbuds, Clear Sound, Single Driver, Secure In-Ear Fit, Detachable Cable, Durable Quality, Compatible with Apple & Android Devices - Blue These sound great. I don't have golden ears, but I believe I can at least partly tell the difference between good and bad headphones/earbud. I loved my last pair, sony buds that I only replaced because the cord finally gave in after probably 6 or 7 years.

The complaints about putting these in are founded, but honestly, if you spend a little time practising, it's not complicated and you can find easier ways. Sometimes I'll put the cord over the ear first, then fold the bud into the canal. Other time, the opposite. I tug on my lobe with the thumb and ring finger and use my index finger to apply pressure on the body of the plug to seat it in my canal.

I do run with these in. They block a lot of sound, but not everything. I' pretty hyper vigilant about my surrounding when I'm running, so I'm usually very aware anyway. I wear them to listen to music while working in the workshop and it turned the quite loud combination of my radial arm saw + shop vac into an EXTREMELY manageable background sound, and I could still hear my son yell at me to shut it off when he wanted to ride his bike in the garage - all without taking away too much from the music.

In less than perfect settings, like resting my head against a pillow (or car seat) they do start to hurt a bit after about an hour. General wear, however, hasn't really had that effect.

The cord doesn't tangle remotely as much as my previous pair, but I hope to keep up the habit of winding them and putting them in the pouch that comes with them.
I got the "black", but they are transparent black. I'd rather opaque, but really, it's not a big deal.
I do sometimes wish the distance between the "Y" where the L/R cords connect was a little longer, again, it's not bothered me enough to dock points, really.
I'd actually give a 4.5/5 but don't feel the need to take away an entire star.

(Update)
7 months it made it without a hitch. Then the right side started to flake on me. I have to contort the wire and get lucky to get sound, which usually stays fine until I remove them and have to do it again the nest time I use them. I'll be returning to Shure for a replacement, but I have to say that my previous Sony pair, with near daily use, lasted 6-7 YEARS without issue, so this bothers me. I'm certain Shure will replace at least the cable, otherwise I'd be dropping more than the one star I took off. I'll update if I have other issues with the replacement process or otherwise.
text_fidelity_b: Shure AONIC 215 Wired Sound Isolating Earbuds, Clear Sound, Single Driver, Secure In-Ear Fit, Detachable Cable, Durable Quality, Compatible with Apple & Android Devices - Blue

text_fidelity_a:
Fire Tablet with Alexa, 7" Display, 16 GB, Blue - with Special Offers (Previous Generation - 5th) My top ten include dogs, sewing machines, houses, my bed, a few trips, and my Kindle. I love my Kindle so much that I actually bought a Kindle edition of a big, heavy, expensive book that I have in hardback just so I don't have to carry it around. It has taken just one month for me to only want to read with the Kindle. It's going to save lots of bookshelf space, my bookshelves are jammed. I love being able to use the dictionary and look up many more words than I used to. Yes, you know the meaning from the context, but it's fun to know the etymology. I took Latin many years ago and frequently consider the root meanings of words, and having the Kindle dictionary makes this easier. Wikipedia is wonderful, too. I looked up the Magna Charta while I was reading a book that mentioned it, and found when it was written, what it was about, etc. I have also looked up some cities to find demographic and weather information.
The ability to change font size and page justification is a good feature. It is important to realize, however, that you can't change justification if the book wasn't formatted to allow that. You get those giant gaps on some lines when it's in full justification. If you use a small font, it's not so bad. Most of the books I have purchased allow left justification, and my guess is that more and more books will be formatted that way, which generally eliminates those gaps. You can get the first chapters of books as free samples, and see how they are formatted, as well as whether you like them as far as writing and subject is concerned.
The next thing I plan to do is put some of my music from my iPod onto the Kindle so I can listen to background music while I read. I understand you can't control the order of the songs, so I'm only going to put on classical music that is not distracting in and of itself.
Getting more books fast is great, too. I forget the name for the phobia that is the fear of running out of things to read, but I have a small case of that, and Kindle is the cure.
Traveling is much nicer when you don't have ten books in your book bag.
I'm asking for an SD card for Christmas from one of the grandkids (it's very inexpensive) so that the Kindle will have even greater capacity.
When you go to the Kindle store from your Kindle, there will be recommendations based on what you have bought, just like there are when you go to Amazon online. However, online you can say "not interested," but on the Kindle, you can't. You get the same recommendations over and over. It would be nice if you could delete recommendations from your Kindle. But, hey, that is definitely just a small thing.
Another thing that would be nice is a password for 1-click ordering from the Kindle.
I'm retired and on a relatively small income. If I lost my Kindle and couldn't afford another one, I would go back to work just long enough to get the money to replace it. That should tell you how much I love it, 'cause I sure don't want to work anymore!
text_fidelity_b: Fire Tablet with Alexa, 7" Display, 16 GB, Blue - with Special Offers (Previous Generation - 5th)

text_fidelity_a:
Surge Protector Power Strip with USB, Silicone Extension Cord with 10 Outlets 3 USB Charging Ports and 1 USB-C Charging Port, 1875W/15A Overload Surge Protection, Gift for Mother's Day PROS

1. It has 10 sockets/outlets.
2. Two of the sockets are offset from the other six. This allows them to be used for wide plugs, which is an important feature, because wide plugs are a frequent occurrence on appliances.
3. The color is an attractive but neutral black which makes the strip fade into the background more than the strips I own which are white or beige.
4. In addition to being a power strip, it also provides surge protection.
5. There are four USB ports that can be used for charging devices. One of them is a USB-C port and the other 3 are standard USB ports. The manufacturer claims in the manual that the three standard USB ports are “smart” USB ports.

CONS

1. I am not entirely comfortable trusting the “smart” USB ports on this device for charging. I feel more comfortable using a regular USB charging adapter and plugging it into a socket on the surge protector side of this device.

2. Regarding the smart USB ports, there are not adequate instructions either in the manual or on the manufacturer’s website that clearly explain the implications of this feature and how to utilize it. I cannot find information on the top mA it supports in charging.

GENERAL INFORMATION ON USB CHARGING

In order to test this device for my Vine review, I spent over two hours (!!!) trying to find comprehensible information on what the term “smart” means in the context of a USB port on a power strip like this one. Unfortunately, I was left with more questions than answers, for which hassle I’m dropping a star off this review. I’ve included some of what I learned below, for what it might be worth to any fellow Amazon customer who might be thinking of purchasing this product.

A smart USB charger port supposedly can, in and of itself, figure out what the optimal charging speed of a specific device is when it is plugged into that port, in order to neither overload it with too much current or under-deliver to it the optimal current. The question on everyone’s mind these days (it certainly has been on mine), is whether it is possible to destroy the battery in a particular device by slamming too much current into it. Apparently, the answer to this all-important question is: No. If, for example, you take a phone which comes with a 900mA wall charger, and you plug it into a 2,100mA charger that comes with a different device you own, it will not damage the phone. It will only speed up the length of time it takes for the phone’s battery to charge. However, if you have a USB device older than 2007, it may not charge on any USB ports newer than the (now ancient), 500mA USB 1.0 and 2.0 PC ports. Which means such older devices may not charge even on the “smart” USB ports on this device.

USB charging current is measured in mA (milliampere, 1/1000 of an ampere, the basic unit for measuring electrical current). There are three kinds of USB ports which are defined by their current specs: a standard downstream port, a charging downstream port, and a dedicated charging port. The first two are found on a desktop computer. The third kind is a “dumb” wall charger.

USB 1.0 and 2.0 standard downstream ports on a computer can deliver up to 500mA (0.5A).

USB 3.0 standard downstream ports on a computer can deliver up to 900mA (0.9A).

USB 3.1 and USB 3.2 ports can deliver between 1,500mA (1.5A) and 3,000mA (3A).

Charging downstream USB ports on a computer can deliver up to 1,500mA (1.5A).

Dedicated USB charging ports on a computer can deliver up to 3,000mA (3A).
text_fidelity_b: Surge Protector Power Strip with USB, Silicone Extension Cord with 10 Outlets 3 USB Charging Ports and 1 USB-C Charging Port, 1875W/15A Overload Surge Protection, Gift for Mother's Day

text_fidelity_a:
co2CREA Hard Case with Sleep Mode Replacement for Apple AirPods Max Headphone (Black Case + Inside Red) This is a smart case - no bra needed.

UPDATE: Wrong, alas. I mean, it’s possible to make this case put your headphones to sleep – at least with the version of this case that I have – but it’s such a precise, finicky, painstaking endeavor that it’s nowhere near worth the effort. I’ve taken to using my case just like everybody else does: with the bra inside.

My guess is that what these third-party case makers need to do is what Apple did with the bra: rather than a couple of dime-sized round magnets, they need to put in long, thin magnets that will connect with the sensors in the earcups no matter where in the case they fall. The bra puts the headphones to sleep every time without fail and without the user having to spend several minutes massaging the headphones into just exactly the perfect position so that they’ll go to sleep, so it can be done; the third-party case manufacturers just haven’t yet figured out how Apple did it.

Anyways: I was dreading this case having an horrendous stench to it, based on several reviews I've read. I'm happy to report that while mine has a smell and it is kind of chemical-y, I find the smell neither strong nor entirely unpleasant. It's pretty mild, strength-wise (and I'm sensitive to such things) and I find the smell has a sort of fresh quality to it, despite its chemical nature. Lucky me, I guess. But this, like the Apple bra, is basically half a case. You need the bra to put the headphones to sleep, and this case to give them adequate protection. Hard to believe in this day and age, but there it is. I guess if Apple included a case with these that did everything necessary they would probably charge an additional $200 for it…

text_fidelity_a:
Sony SSCSE Dolby Atmos Enabled Speakers, Black, Dolby Atmos Enabled Speakers (Pair), 4 Inch (Pack of 2) I found it odd, reading some of these reviews, which claimed that these Sonys were definitely better than the Pioneer BS22s. Very odd indeed. It makes me wonder if they either weren't directly comparing the two back and forth, or didn't have the Pioneers set up properly: ~6 feet apart, toed in toward the listener, ear level, grills off.

To my ears, the Sonys aren't much better than the Micca MB42x. They both have slightly elevated treble, and are rather thin and one-note sounding in their presentation. Not a lot of depth or punch.

The BS22s however, you really "feel" the music. The soundstage is very open, and everything sounds larger even though the woofers are only 4" compared to the 5-1/4" SSCS5s. There is depth and a musicality that just can't be matched by the Sonys, and it's apparent right away. It's like they almost disappear and you're just left with the music. Most speakers in this price range are going to sound similar to the SSCS5/MB42x, not many if any are going to sound like the Pioneers.

I must have switched back and forth 200-300 times comparing the two, trying to convince myself that the Sonys were better than they were. I got them at $73 and the BS22s at $99, so I really wanted to like the SSCS5s.

It was always obvious which speaker was superior though - not once did I say "oh, the Sonys really sound better here". That's not to say these are bad speakers, but I don't think they're worth much more than $73, the sale price. The Pioneers however I'd be willing to pay their retail price and a bit more. If you're really on a budget, you could be satisfied with these ~$73, especially if you're only concerned about watching movies. But if you are willing to pay $20 more for the Pioneers when they're on sale (or even at $129), I'd recommend it.

Just remember to set the BS22s up properly: ~6 feet apart, toed in toward the listener, ear level, grills off. Also make sure they're properly amped.

The SSCS5s are decent and cheap enough that I decided to use my old receiver with them at my computer. I'd probably prefer them over the MB42X slightly, but that's about it.

With a budget sub like the Dayton SUB-1200 properly placed (subwoofer crawl) along with the BS22s, you'll have a system that sounds very nice and hits above its weight class - trust me on that. It used to be that headphones were a cheaper investment than speakers and you could get a better sound for less, but this set up edges out my HE-500/Bifrost/Asgard 2 and it's actually cheaper. Didn't think that was possible.
text_fidelity_b: Sony SSCSE Dolby Atmos Enabled Speakers, Black, Dolby Atmos Enabled Speakers (Pair), 4 Inch (Pack of 2)

text_fidelity_a:
Apple 12.9-inch iPad Pro Wi-Fi + Cellular - 12.9" Tablet - 256 GB - 3G/4G - GOLD There is so much talk about the declining sales of iPad. So much so, the discussion might influence a potential buyer to pause before buying or not buy at all, and instead buy a competing tablet or laptop. I think the key to making a decision to buy the iPad Pro lies in a wallpaper Apple provided with the very first version of iPad. It was a licensed photograph of Pyramid Lake by Robert Misrach. The exposure, made at night, appears to be in daylight. The clue that it was a night time photograph are the star trails that resulted from the long exposure. The lake surface appears as smooth as a mirror. The mirror surface of the lake in this photograph enables the viewer to immerse himself or herself in the device, making it a perfect fulfillment of whatever there desires might be "for iPad". The iPad is a perfect "evocative object", evoking whatever feelings and intentions the iPad user brings to it. That is why the iPad is so undefinable and uncategorizable. It is is whatever ever we want it to be.....and with iPad Pro Apple reaches again for that elusive quality.

After 7 days with the new Apple iPad Pro I am happy that I followed my hunch that the iPad Pro would be better for me than a laptop for a mobile multi-purpose device. I am very pleased how the slide over multitasking works. Bigger is better whether using multi-tasking features live slide over and picture-in-picture. The user does not get poorly sized Windows for both applications. For example if your browser is open in one window, and photos is open in a second, but applications are scaled to size in each window.

I purchased the 32MB version because I tend to use iCloud to store photos, music, documents. I only need local storage for IOS apps and the few documents I need.

I purchased a black rear cover, and a contrasting white front cover. The only accessory I use so far is the Apple Pencil for drawing in Paper by 53 and Apple Notes ( to take notes in my University classes ). I use the iPad Pro almost exclusively landscape or horizontal, the only iPad that can be used in portrait is the Mini. At the time I purchased the iPad Pro the wait times for shipment of the Apple Pencil was 4-5 weeks. However, I was able to find one locally at my University Bookstore. I am concentrating on using the Apple Pencil at the moment, using just the on-screen keyboard. I have an open mind about buying the iPad Pro keyboard in the future. However, the iPad is all about creating art through use of touch and the pencil right now. I don't want it to be a laptop. I want it to be a "blank sheet of paper".

The audio produced by the 4 speakers produce a very pleasing music listening experience without headphones.

One final note: it appears the iPad Pro includes technology that can be used in the future today's blog post in Daring Fireball notes that the Lightning connector includes support for USB 3.0, a much faster transfer speeds. It will be interesting to see what applications take advantage of that speed next year.
text_fidelity_b: Apple 12.9-inch iPad Pro Wi-Fi + Cellular - 12.9" Tablet - 256 GB - 3G/4G - GOLD

EarFun Wireless Earbuds, [2020 CES Award] Free Bluetooth 5.0 Earbuds with Wireless Charging Case, USB-C Quick Charge, IPX7 Waterproof in-Ear Wireless Headphones, Deep Bass, 30H Playtime I purchased these after reading a review (CNet, I believe) about the best earbuds. I'd been looking for wired ones because I've bought nice, top-end Bluetooth earbuds before and have never been happy with them. Usually, they don't work consistently, are subject to interference, drop the audiobook/podcast/call, and are too finicky.
These, though? They've exceeded even my highest hopes. The sound quality is excellent. They have a wonderful case that charges them until its battery dies, which then recharges quickly with its included USB-C charger cord (no plug, you need a regular USB port to plug it into).
They're super comfortable, they stay in my ears impressively well, you can wear one at a time if you'd like because they connect independently and each has the pause/play button on it. They have an impressive range, too. I've accidentally walked away from my phone and made it 4 rooms away without losing the sound (it does get a little fuzzy). I've used them frequently since I purchased them 3 months ago and I'm still super impressed. Reliable, excellent, and I'm no longer looking for wired earbuds. I highly recommend them. The one downside for me is that they're noise-canceling. I'd love it if there was an option not to, but to make up for it, I just wear one when I'm out walking or need to listen for something.
text_fidelity_b: EarFun Wireless Earbuds, [2020 CES Award] Free Bluetooth 5.0 Earbuds with Wireless Charging Case, USB-C Quick Charge, IPX7 Waterproof in-Ear Wireless Headphones, Deep Bass, 30H Playtime

text_fidelity_a:
ASUS MeMO Pad FHD 10 ME302C-A1-BL 10.1-Inch 16GB Tablet (Blue) I've used a Chromebook, I've used various Kindles, but this is my first experience with a tablet. The Android OS is still pretty alien to me, and I'm still knocking around in it, discovering how it works. So it's probably not fair to review the tablet itself based on my own inexperience with the OS. But this tablet is high resolution, easy on the eyes, and amply large. I love that it senses the ambient lighting and adjusts automatically, because my Kindles don't do that and I have to take the brightness up and down manually.

One thing I don't like about it is that it does not use Flash so you can't play anything that requires Flash. Any attempts to add Flash give you messages that Google or Adobe have decommissioned Flash and will not use it. I spent several hours nosing around in the forums looking for a solution, and even found some cautions that I could hurt my tablet by trying to install a Flash player, so I didn't do it. Sure, geeks and power users may laugh at this, but I don't want to mess with it. But what this means is that I cannot watch Amazon Prime movies on this tablet, which is a real bummer. In the forums I found discussions about this; it's apparently a problem with Amazon, not anybody else. They have not developed an app to allow playing their instant videos on Android systems. Somebody said they were hoping an app would be out by 2014, but that there was no guarantee; that Amazon is probably trying to protect its Kindle market by not releasing an app. So my normally high estimation of Amazon is knocked down a peg for absence of an app. Hopefully they will rememdy this soon.

The first thing I did was order a rooCase for it, but I discovered that the cut-out in the rooCase for the rear-facing camera vignetted photos and videos (imagine a black circle around the edges). So I took the plunge and ordered [[ASIN:B00BP54KNM ASUS Official Folio Keyboard Case for MeMOPad Smart ME301 Series]], and that's given me a completely different experience with this tablet. It feels more like my Chromebook, if a little less stable in my lap. I like the soft-touch ON button on the Folio keyboard case because, without it, it's kind of hard to turn on the tablet. There are a few Bluetooth connection issues with the Folio keyboard case, but that's for another review.

One thing that is weird to me about this tablet is that you are not supposed to leave it plugged in to the charger. I'm used to leaving my Kindles plugged in overnight, but with the Asus tablet you're only supposed to leave it plugged in for eight hours at most. (And if you get the Folio keyboard case for it, you use the same charger for both, one after the other.) The screen is more responsive to touch than my Kindle Fire, but still there is sometimes a lag that I haven't quite gotten used to yet. I think it's like learning to drive a new car: you just have to get used to the way it handles, and then you can groove right on into it.

It is definitely easier on the eyes than a 7" screen. Again, the auto-adjusting brightness is a major boon. I love that I can pick it up in the middle of the night, read or browse for a while, then close it up in its case (which auto-offs) and go back to sleep. I'm still not sure I'm in love with the whole tablet concept, but Google Voice definitely makes it easier to use it. For the money, I think this Asus offering is a very good value.
text_fidelity_b: ASUS MeMO Pad FHD 10 ME302C-A1-BL 10.1-Inch 16GB Tablet (Blue)

text_fidelity_a:
Kindle Oasis E-reader with Leather Charging Cover - Black, 6" High-Resolution Display (300 ppi), Wi-Fi + Free Cellular Connectivity, Built-In Audible (Previous Generation - 8th) “I wonder how long it has been we readers have gazed at the young person sitting under a tree at night reading a book on the Kindle home screen..oh, our love affair with books and being able to read our stories late into the night…...by candlelight….anywhere.”

Pre-release technology reviewers commenting on the price of the Kindle Oasis are wrong. The new Kindle Oasis is worth the the price Amazon is charging, including cover it hardly represents at all an increase in price when compared with a Kindle Voyage with cover. Yet it provides the two most asked for improvements in mobile devices: increased battery life reducing the need to frequently recharge, and improved screen legibility (new sans-serif Ember font, and more LEDS that provide increased brightness).

“When we are immersed into the story of our favorite books, only that world matters.”

Pre-release technology reviewers have compared the Kindle as a single purpose e-reader, to multipurpose devices like in smartphones, tablets and computers. When we choose to read, we are seeking a bit of solitude in the day and night. Oh, how easy it is to remember being annoyed with yet another incoming phone call, text message or email. The power of focus!

“The tactile feel of a book”

Pre-release technology reviewer have labelled the Kindle as luxurious with it’s leather cover. How soon we forget our books covered with leather! And we are willing to pay an extra price for it!

As I sit across the street from the one and only Amazon retail store “in the world”, I have unboxed and set up my new Kindle Oasis. Maybe I am one of the few ordinary people outside of Amazon and the technology press in the world to have been able to purchase one so soon. The feeling reminds me of going to a release party in the same shopping center for the latest Harry Potter novel.

This Kindle is new, like the latest release from our favorite author.

It connects me to reading anywhere, late at night when there is little light.

The Kindle Oasis is magical.
text_fidelity_b: Kindle Oasis E-reader with Leather Charging Cover - Black, 6" High-Resolution Display (300 ppi), Wi-Fi + Free Cellular Connectivity, Built-In Audible (Previous Generation - 8th)

It’s one of my two favorite ones (the other is the Jam Heavy Metal) and outside of the Jam is far better sound quality than the several others I own. If you’re looking for something that gives you “adequate” music and can handle a splash or two, this is overkill. But if you want rich sound and insurance against big rain (or worse, a dunk in a pool), it’s probably worth moving up to this one.

Pros:
IP67, highly water-resistant. I confess, I didn’t test this by submerging it as it says you can; I’m gonna just trust ‘em on this one

Rich, distortion-free sound. Despite its size, this can get quite loud (in a nice touch for those wishing to pump it up, the volume controls on the speaker, unlike most I own, work independently of your source device (i.e. you can max out your iphone volume and then in addition max out the speaker). Even at high volume the sound doesn’t distort. And the bass is powerful and thick (not sub-woofer but then, if you want that, get a sub-woofer. For a portable speaker, it’s perhaps the best bass I’ve heard). It’s also quite clear. In comparison to the Jam, I’d say the bass on this is better but the Jam just edges out in terms of clarity with treble/voice. The sound quality is also quite good as a speaker phone.

Connecting. Pairing via Bluetooth was pretty instantaneous with my iPhone and iPad. There’s also an audio-jack to plug in

Stereo potential. You can link it with another, though I don’t have a second so can’t speak to how it sounds

Size: it’s small enough to toss easily into a backpack if not a pocket. Has a heft to it in terms of a quality, durable build-feel, but not so as to strain you carrying it around at all.

Cons are all pretty minor
Buttons are a bit stiff (maybe this will change)

No charging cable with mine

Neutral: no connectivity with voice activation like Alexa
Charges in a few hours and last anywhere from 8-12 depending on volume, not the best but far from the worst

Personally, I hate tinny, thin-sounding speakers. If I’m going to listen to music, I don’t need it to be pristine, but I do want it to sound like my music, so I think this is a good value. The sound quality alone is worth it—it blows away cheaper Bluetooth portables— and combined with the high-level water resistance, it’s makes it an even easier recommendation
text_fidelity_b: Denon DSB-250BT Envaya Portable Bluetooth 8.25” Speaker (Black) - Lightweight, Waterproof & Dustproof | Up to 13 Hours of Battery Life | Hands-Free Phone Calling | Voice Compatibility with Siri

text_fidelity_a:
Microsoft Surface Book 13.5" (Intel Core i5, 8GB RAM, 256 GB) We have a number of surface tablets in our house, and this was my first surface book. I got it hoping for some increased performance for using with my landscape CAD program, and I did notice a difference in the smoothness when working with CAD on this device as opposed to my other comparable surface tablets. The better performance only works when it is hooked up to the keyboard, which is fine for CAD work.

I also like to use this as a tablet for photo editing work related to my business, and here I noticed my number one complaint about this device, which is that the tablet part itself does not have the little foldout stand that all of the other surface tablets have. I guess they think that you will just connect it to the keyboard, but sometimes I want it to be as flexible and lightweight as a regular surface Pro tablet, and while you can unhook it from the keyboard and use it as a tablet, it feels more bulky and the lack of stand makes it less flexible in its use than the surface Pro tablets.

One thing I did notice is that you can connect it to the keyboard backwards and use the keyboard as a stand that way, however that does not bend to the same angle as the tablet stands do on a regular surface Pro.

I also think that the battery life is a lot less on this one than on the surface Pro tablets. Even when not connected to the keyboard and the increased computing performance that you get from that, it seems to wear down its batteries on tablet mode in about 30 to 45 minutes of photo editing. When I worked on my surface tablet in this fashion, I feel like I got a little less than two hours before having to recharge.

Overall, if you plan to use this primarily plugged in as a laptop and only occasionally as a tablet, the increased performance from the attached keyboard make this a worthwhile choice if you do gaming or more high-powered computing. However, if you are primarily using it as a tablet or in places where battery life is a critical consideration, I would suggest the regular surface Pro tablet instead.

In terms of accessories, I use the surface pen constantly, but haven't reached for the other accessories much at all. The surface pen makes it so smooth to make notes on photographs to convey ideas to people, and is great for photo editing.
text_fidelity_b: Microsoft Surface Book 13.5" (Intel Core i5, 8GB RAM, 256 GB)

Blink Outdoor Camera Wall Mount Bracket, Hard Protective Case and Metal Mount for Blink XT2 Cameras Weather Proof Adjustable Indoor Outdoor Mount and Cover for Blink Home Security(3 Pack, Black) When I installed my Blink XT2, I found I needed to move it a little lower so I could maybe see the face of the delivery person. Thinking I could unscrew the mount without removing the camera, I turned the camera to one side so I could access the screws. The camera fell to the floor. A little bit of friction is not sufficient to hold these cameras. That is when I started looking at these mounts which SHOULD be included in the box.

This is in several parts. Plastic camera-enclosing parts are held together with 4 small screws. The metal part is attached to the wall with 3 flat-head #6 screws.

Unscrew the adjusting part so the base of the mount can be attached to the wall. Do not try to adjust the angle unless this part is loose. Use care when tightening the screws - do it manually so the screws are not over-tightened. The aluminum base could be cracked by over-tightening.

The small screws that are used to attach the back cover to the front should be machine screws, and the posts into which they are screwed should be metal. This is my opinion and is because these screws will have to be removed and reinstalled every time the batteries are replaced.

One piece of plastic had a small 'tab' on it that had to be cut off before the back cover would attach to the front.

A hole in the bottom of the plastic is there to allow a charging cable to be attached. If you do not plan to use rechargeable batteries and have no need for the USB cable, plug the hole so insects do not go inside looking for a new home. I used a small piece of closed cell foam packing material (photo).

If you want to use these mounts with the earlier Blink cameras, you might want to use some foam so the camera does not move around inside the enclosure (photo).
text_fidelity_b: Blink Outdoor Camera Wall Mount Bracket, Hard Protective Case and Metal Mount for Blink XT2 Cameras Weather Proof Adjustable Indoor Outdoor Mount and Cover for Blink Home Security(3 Pack, Black)

Toshiba TransMemory Pro USB 3.0 Flash Drive (PFU064U-1BDS) With its huge 64GB file storage capacity, this flash drive can theoretically store the entire contents of a PC's hard drive and its operating system. Since I don't have that many files to store on an everyday basis, I am reserving this flash drive to store high-resolution videos and other RAM-eating monster files.

For $80, this is rather overpriced. There are USB drives that are cheaper and will do the job just as well. To make the USB look like it's worth the extra price, Toshiba made the casing unnecessarily oversized - there's no practical reason why the USB case had to be so wide (you will have trouble sticking another USB drive next to it, which is annoying). It's a gimmick to impress the user, nothing more. However, when you hold it in your hand, it's not as heavy as the metallic finish would lead you to believe - it's actually very lightweight, and to be honest, feels cheap. I have questions of its durability, despite the fancy advertising.

To test, I copied all the videos I had stored in my PC to see how fast it would be to store all of them on this monster drive. I was disappointed that the saving time was not noticeably faster, which may not be the fault of the USB drive but rather my computer. However, I have to say it was a relief that I never got the "you don't have enough memory" message, so you can count on this USB to store tons of videos you can't find room for elsewhere.

The only drawback to this single-USB method of storage is that I don't feel entirely comfortable saving so much stuff on just ONE drive, despite its capacity. It's equivalent to putting all your eggs in one basket - what if you lose that single USB - you're screwed. Though convenient, I'd rather spread out my back-up files, so if you use this USB to save a huge file, I'd buy more than one just to be safe.

The other thing I thought was unnecessary was the included encryption software that's included on the drive. You only see it when you open up the Files folder, and there are two lengthy PDFs with instructions on how to activate the password and security options. Fortunately you do not require to activate them in order to use the drive - I've never found I needed such security measures, but if you plan to store financial data on this USB, it's a good feature.

Lastly, I hate the fact that, unlike my other drives, it has a cap. I am forever losing the caps to my flash drives and have since opted to buy only the retractable ones, where you can slide the connector in or out. Too bad this one doesn't have it, otherwise I would have added a star.

So, in short, a mixed review. Give me a drive that's cheaper, that's big on the inside but small on the outside, capless, and I'd buy more of them.
text_fidelity_b: Toshiba TransMemory Pro USB 3.0 Flash Drive (PFU064U-1BDS)

text_fidelity_a:
Sony A90J 65 Inch TV: BRAVIA XR OLED 4K Ultra HD Smart Google TV with Dolby Vision HDR and Alexa Compatibility XR65A90J- 2021 Model The box took a big gouge in shipping (in just the original TV box), but the TV was fine, so packaging is probably adequate. Unboxing was easy and there was just a bit of styrofoam and minimal cardboard. Be careful with removing the television from the box, because these things are getting thin enough to be bent under their own weight.

It mounted fine on my old wall mount, but required a different screw size. The screws from my previous setup were the wrong size, so you might want to check what you've got and order some so you don't have to wait around.

There isn't much thought put into cable management, so you'll have to come up with your own solution if you don't want cords visible. Power cord is in the lower right quadrant. Most of the other cords are in the lower left, as is a well hidden power button on the back left. The instructions are minimal. I tried hooking my receiver in as instructed to use the television speaker in place of my old center speaker, but it wouldn't work. It may have just been a clash of brands and standards, because every time I tried to switch to using the TV speakers in the options, it would shut off my Pioneer receiver instead. I ended up using the other speaker input, which did work. I can't believe we're in the 2020's and still cramming bare wires in as audio input. I've got a drawer full of various audio cables here.

Turning it on, I was greeted with setup options. The remote seems high quality, but I wish it had some air-remote functionality. Navigating menus with buttons can get a bit confusing. After getting it hooked up to wifi, I was off to YouTube to find something to make sure it was working right before I hooked everything else up. One of those HD coral reef relaxation videos was just the thing. The picture is vibrant! Bright and colorful. The bezels aren't small enough to tile these together, but are very small. My kids wouldn't let me change the video for hours. They just sat and watched the fish. I'm susceptible to the whine some televisions put out, and I've heard none of that. Worked great for video games, though I didn't try anything especially high end. Worked well for computer output. With the exception of that one audio jack compatibility issue, and the different sized screws, everything has worked as expected.

The screen is a speaker, like a modern smartphone. Sound is good, especially at frequencies you would hear from a center speaker. I definitely still wanted my subwoofer and side speakers to round things out, but it's really nice to have the voices from the television coming from where the faces are, not from some speaker below the television.

I don't have a different brand of 2021 television to compare it to, but my impression is that there is a bit of a premium for the brand name, but it's a very nice product. This was certainly an upgrade for me. A lot of progress has been made in the 8 years since I last upgraded.
text_fidelity_b: Sony A90J 65 Inch TV: BRAVIA XR OLED 4K Ultra HD Smart Google TV with Dolby Vision HDR and Alexa Compatibility XR65A90J- 2021 Model

text_fidelity_a:
Polaroid Cube+ 1440p Mini Lifestyle Action Camera with Wi-Fi & Image Stabilization (Red) I really hate to use the word “cute” but there’s no way around it – this is a cute cam! It looks pretty much the same as the original Cube, but offers improved video and the addition of WiFi. Of the new features, the WiFi is the most significant, and makes this far more useful as a cam.

I also have the original Cube and the build quality continues to be very good. These are priced higher than the “no name” action cams, but after using (and breaking) a couple of those, it’s nice to be able to count on the Cube to keep on working. It’s water resistant, which makes it less worrisome when using it in bad weather or around water. It supports up to a 128MB SD card

The form factor and overall design is much the same as the original Cube. It has a magnet in the base that is more than strong enough to keep it well-planted. It’s not strong enough for significant activity (e.g., staying on a bike handle while riding) but it offers the benefit of tripod-like stability without the need for a tripod (providing you have something metal to fasten the magnet).

The biggest change is wifi on the Cube+. I found the setup to be straightforward – basically just download the app and follow the setup steps. I love that the app lets you use it as a live view – that’s a big improvement over the original Cube. It’s a very helpful feature for planning a shot, plus allows me to monitor how things are turning out without having to play the video.

Image quality has been impressive – zero complaints there. I was pleased with the resolution of the original Cube, and this is a bit better. Audio quality is OK. It’s not outstanding, but it clearly picks up voices. I understand that earlier versions of the Cube+ had very poor sound quality, but the one I have (got it in Dec 2015) is fine with regard to sound.

All in all, it’s a great cam with a fun form factor and look. Well worth considering if you’re looking for a small profile action cam with solid build quality and performance. While the price has increased over that of the original Cube, the wifi features are very useful and well implemented, making this version well worth the additional cost.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: Polaroid Cube+ 1440p Mini Lifestyle Action Camera with Wi-Fi & Image Stabilization (Red)

Lifeproof FRĒ SERIES iPhone 6/6s Waterproof Case (4.7" Version) - Retail Packaging - SUNSET (PIPELINE/WINDSURF/LONGBOARD) I got my mother the Lifeproof FRE case for her iPhone 6. For the last year, she’s been using a cheap case I bought on Amazon, the Diztronic Voyeur Case. I didn’t feel it was protective enough, so I hoped the Lifeproof FRE would work for her.

Unfortunately, she didn’t like the case at all, and wanted it off her phone minutes after I put it on. I made her use it for a few weeks, and while she didn’t experience any sound problems, there were several quality of life things that sealed the dislike for the Lifeproof FRE case.

PRO:
—The built-in screen protector is pretty good. I liked that I didn’t have to install it myself, as it’s part of the case.

CONS:
—Within minutes of putting the Lifeproof FRE case on her phone, I dropped it. The back of the case is slick, some kind of hard plastic instead of the grippier TPU case. The Lifeproof case just didn’t feel nice to hold in my hand, and with the slicker plastic, I worried that my mom would drop her phone as well.

—The little “door” that protects the charger port was super hard for her to open. Every time my mom wanted to charge her phone, I had to come do it for her, since she couldn’t get the door open. I understand needing a tight seal for the waterproof protection, but there has to be an easier way to access the charger port.

—The small oval cut out for charging cords was too small for my non Apple Lightning cables. I have two that are Apple certified, AmazonBasics and Zerolemon, and neither fit.

—My mom found it impossible to manipulate any of the buttons. I assume the buttons will loosen up over months, but boy, they are super hard to press when the case is new.

My mom’s not quite the intended audience for the case, but as she plans to keep her iPhone for a few years, we want it to stay in nice shape. And you never know when you’re going to drop your phone into a snowbank or puddle, so having a waterproof case adds peace of mind. But I’ll have to keep looking for her, because the Lifeproof FRE had a couple of little problems that added up to big annoyances.
text_fidelity_b: Lifeproof FRĒ SERIES iPhone 6/6s Waterproof Case (4.7" Version) - Retail Packaging - SUNSET (PIPELINE/WINDSURF/LONGBOARD)

text_fidelity_a:
Google Pixel Slate 12.3-Inch 2 in 1 Tablet Intel Core i5, 8GB RAM, 128GB, Aspect Ratio 3:2 The Pixel Slate is Google's computer of the near future. It is great for some people right now, but not for everyone. Google has had their Android tablets and Chromebooks for many years now. The Pixel Slate combines those two concepts into an evolving platform. The hardware is really great right now with great fit-and-finish, a very sharp colorful screen, very responsive touch sensors, and great sound quality. Battery life is very good (over 10 hours per charge). The software is evolving quickly. Google has already released many updates the Chrome operating system and I expect this to continue.

The main problem with the software is that the Pixel Slate is running two types of apps: Chrome browser web-apps and Android apps. The user interfaces for these two are slightly different, which can lead to user confusion. There are also interoperability problems between the two, which also leads to user confusion. For example, Android apps can share files by just clicking on the share icon. Sharing a file from a web-app to an Android app requires downloading the app to the local file system, then opening the Android app and hunting through the file system to find and open the file. Hopefully one day some kind of automatic sharing mechanism will be implemented. Another confusion is that some web-apps and Android apps have the same name and functionality, but don't work the same. For example, Amazon Kindle has both a web-app and an Android app. If I download a book in the Kindle Android app, the Kindle web-app cannot find it, so I have to remember to use the Kindle Android app.

Who should buy a Pixel Slate? Google initially announced 4 versions of this product: one with a Celeron CPU, one with a Core m3 CPU, one with a Core i5 CPU, and one with a Core i7 CPU. I have the i5 version, which is plenty fast and responsive for anything I'm trying to do (I am not a gamer).

Apparently, the performance of the Celeron version was so bad that product has been cancelled. Prices now range from $800 to $1600, not including accessories like the keyboard or stylus. Even the $800 version is a lot of money, especially when you consider that a very good Chromebook can be had for much less money and that has a built-in keyboard. I have to imagine that the only people who should consider the Pixel Slate instead of a high-end Chromebook are people who will regularly need to use this device as a lightweight tablet. At just a pound or so, the Pixel Slate's tablet mode is much lighter weight and much less bulky than any Chromebook, even those flip-over style Chromebooks. If you can't imagine life without a physical keyboard, then get yourself a good Chromebook instead of the Pixel Slate.

The physical keyboard is not included with the Pixel Slate. Amazon sells a couple of different versions, but both have flaws, as well as very high prices. For now, I'm using a Belkin USB keyboard when I'm using the Pixel Slate at my desk. When I'm on the go, I use the tablet in touch screen mode without a physical keyboard. If a better physical keyboard comes along, I'll rethink this setup.
text_fidelity_b: Google Pixel Slate 12.3-Inch 2 in 1 Tablet Intel Core i5, 8GB RAM, 128GB, Aspect Ratio 3:2

Packaging: Easily unpackaged, not too excessive

Charging: Mine came nearly fully charged. From whatever point it was at, it took about 7 or 8 minutes to reach full charge. I'll update with how long the charge lasts and how long to charge an empty battery once I get to that point

Pairing: Couldn't be easier, simpler, or faster. Turned it one, went to my bluetooth on my IOS devices (sorry, that's all I have so can't say what the Android experience is), and there it was. Worked seamlessly and immediately with all my devices and my laptop, both single-user mode and multi-party mode. Everything should pair so easily. Range was excellent--was bale to use it from every room on the same floor (didn't check it between floors)

Footprint/build: it's small (you can see the dimensions) and very light. But it delivers surprisingly solid sound with no distortion at the top volume and it feels nicely sturdy and solid despite its lack of real heft. Its sturdiness combined with its material makes me worry-free with regard to how it would hold up being moved around a room or transported from place to place.

sound: as mentioned, surprisingly full. I was really pleased with the volume, the clarity, and the richness of sound.

operation: again, couldn't be simpler. Two clearly marked volume buttons on the top-- + and -. The central bottom button performs several actions depending on if you hold it (change from "indoor" sound to "outdoor" sound) or tap it once or twice.

It connects via bluetooth, NFC, or line-in

In multiplayer mode, you can connect up to five devices and whoever hits play gets to play their music. Worked without a hitch with all five devices I hooked up. I can see this getting a lot of fun use.

Really, a nice piece of tech--good build quality, excellent sound, super ease of use, fun to use. So far it looks like they nailed everything (just waiting to see about the battery life and charging)

text_fidelity_a:
Garmin Nuvi 2595LMT UPDATE: after installing the latest map update and waiting for a very long time for the install software to do its thing and worrying if it had actually finished the install because after about an hour my computer said "the application has unexpectedly quit," the device seems to be working perfectly.

Overall, I like the 2595LMT. It boots and finds the satellites faster and has more information available.

Pros:
1. I can press the lower left "Arrive time" button and change it to a variety of readouts: miles remaining, altitude, time via.
2. Voice command works, mostly, especially on simple commands like "Go Home." More complex commands, like an address, return a wide variety of responses, most of them wrong. (Why it's searching the entire United States when it knows where I am and should be looking locally is beyond me.) I liked the old way of narrowing search to State, then City, then Address. Now it just asks you for the whole address, which it likely doesn't understand.
3. It's slimmer and lighter.
4. Easy to import my favorites from my old Nuvi into the 2595LMT. Using a PC, after plugging the old Nuvi into a computer using the USB port,

a. Navigate until you find the "current.GPX" file on the old Nuvi and
b. Copy it to your desktop (this is also a way to make a backup should you desire.)
c. Rename the file: replace "current" with any word you want, as long as it's not "current") so that it is names "anyword.gpx"
d. Attach the new Nuvi 2595LMT to the computer and navigate until you find the folder with its "current.gpx" file.
e. Copy the "anyword.gpx" file from the desktop into the same folder where the "Current.gpx" file resides.
f. Disconnect and restart. All the old favorites will be added to the current list in your new Nuvi.

5. It doesn't say "recalculating" when you disregard its directions
6. It has lane indicators: a series of arrows in the upper left that tell you which lane to get into to make the next turn. Very cool.
7. Touch screen allows scrolling like a smartphone, at least on some screens.
8. Allows you to add/edit shortcuts like a PC. You can create and move icons around so that you can get to a particular feature with one touch.
9. Micro-SD card only
10. Bigger screen
11. 3-D view of the road
12. Speed limit indicator and simultaneous readout of your actual speed that turns red if you exceed the local speed limit. (I wish it bonged quietly when the speed limit changed to remind you that you have to go slower or can go faster.)

Cons:
1. Sadly, on my unit (even after map and software updates) when I say, "Find Place" it immediately crashes and reboots. And if I say, "Find City" it ignores me, even if I ask it to find New York or Los Angeles. I may try reinstalling the software in case it loaded incompletely for some reason. (UPDATE: I waited a couple of weeks and tried updating the maps again. This time it fully installed and happily all the voice commands now work very well. This alone is a good reason to get is unit. Typing while driving is difficult and dangerous. Voice command is simply wonderful and something I've always wanted in a Garmin.)
2. Stuff has been moved around so that the interface is a bit foreign. For instance, "Favorites" are now "Saved Places" and trying to save or edit a saved place is confusing until you get the hang of it.
3. Doesn't have a powered cradle anymore, only a standard mini-USB on the back. Not a real problem, but it's slower to hook up and remove. I used to be able to drop it on the cradle and go. Now I have to find the end of the cable and thread it into a small port on the back. Minor.
4. The traffic function in my opinion is a joke. Driving LA freeways at most times involves congestion and some delay. It's simply the way it is. The Garmin hates congestion and is constantly trying to get you around it. Thus it's constantly bonging and telling me to get off the freeway to take surface streets, assuming they are magically uncongested when in reality the surface streets during rush hour are ten times worse. I'm pretty much going to ignore its traffic suggestions and may turn it off altogether. If you buy the amazon basics power cord [[ASIN:B003N2POXK AmazonBasics Vehicle Power Cable with Mini-USB Connector for GPS and Other Mini-USB Devices]] it doesn't have a built in traffic receiver and thus defeats the annoying and constant attempts to route you around congestion. Simply put, don't believe the alternate route is going to save you any time. Getting onto surface streets during rush hour is a recipe for even longer delays.
text_fidelity_b: Garmin Nuvi 2595LMT

Sony STR-DN1050 7.2 Channel Hi-Res 4K AV Receiver (Built-in Wi-fi & Bluetooth) Had a STR-DN1040, which we liked. Had no problem getting it up and running in our dedicated home theater. It worked well and sounded great. However, after 8 months the HDMI board went out (common problem we've learned). It was still under warranty, so we sent it off to Sony. Sony was not going to have the parts available for more than a month, so they offered us a brand new STR-DN1050. Sony customer service was excellent and it's hard to knock them when they offer a brand new amp that is the next newer model. We only received the new amp this week, but so far we love it. It was easy to set up and get running. I like the on screen setup display for the amp. It was very easy to navigate through. I know that several reviews I read complained about their being fewer HDMI inputs than the 1040. To us that did not matter as it is in a dedicated media room that only has a Blu-ray, DirecTV, and an iPhone connected to it. It sill has the front HDMI in the event we want to make an impromptu addition, as well more rear HDMI inputs available. I also read about folks complaining that the remote controls less functions. I am content with the new remote, as I didn't really control everything from the stock remote anyway. We really like that when we turn up the volume on the new remote, a volume control is displayed on the video screen. The 1040 did not do that and we missed it since our previous Onkyo did. There were also some concerns that the AMP was not truly 4K compatible. We use an Epson 8350 1080p projector (http://www.amazon.com/Epson-PowerLite-Home-Cinema-Projector/dp/B0044UHJWY/ref=sr_1_1?ie=UTF8&qid=1426790549&sr=8-1&keywords=Epson+8350), so not having full 4K compatibility is not a problem. To us the Blu-ray and DirecTV HD programs look awesome.

For a mid-range/price I would absolutely recommend this amp. Of course you can spend more, but why? Since the last amp went out after 8 mos, I am going to leave this review with 4 stars until we get some time under it's belt.

If you want to make your life and set up so much easier, also get the Deadbolt Banana Plugs, 12-pair, By Sewell Direct: http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B006U3O566/ref=oh_aui_detailpage_o00_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1

text_fidelity_a:
Jabra Move Style Edition, Black – Wireless Bluetooth Headphones with Superior Sounds Quality, Long Battery Life, Ultra-Light and Comfortable Wireless Headphones, 3.5 mm Jack Connector Included First I like sound! I'm an audiophile at heart but in my life now I'm an audiophile on a BUDGET! These are my first bluetooth speakers. More on that in a minute.

I was looking for on ear bluetooth speakers with a budget of about $50 to $60 and was set on waiting for a sale on the JBL EB45T but then saw these recommended on the wirecutter website (a pretty good review site in my opinion)

There is nothing wrong with these, but nothing really right about them either. They have a nice neutral sound that you can listen to for a long time. For movies and youtube on my computer, they are great. But there is nothing in the sound that is going to wow you either. Trust me if there was something actually wrong with the sound, I'd be telling you. You can listen to these for a long time without ear fatigue. If you are looking for lots of rumble for movies, these probably aren't the right phones for you. But if your movie listening requirements are more modest then these work well for that. For casual background music, podcasts, audiobooks, they will work really well for that.

Isolation is not great. I think the plastic is thin so a certain amount of noise gets in. I wanted to be able to hear a little bit of background noise, things going on in the house, but these push my limit for how much I want to hear. Even though they were open-back my Sennheiser HD-229 did a better job with isolation because of the design of the pad.

Comfort isn't bad and for my ears, the ear cup size is just about right size. I wish the earpieces swiveled a bit more but for my head, they swivel just enough. . They have a left and right and the cups swivel so little that if you have them on the wrong way you will notice.

Bluetooth... These are a pain in the backside on Win 7. When I want to use them I have to go and delete the previous pairing, pair them again and then go to the control panel and set these to be used for output. For movies on the computer, they get out of sync. I even set my movie player (Pot Player which I highly recommend) to use the Bluetooth headphones and they still get out of sync with the audio. I don't know if it's the player, the USB Bluetooth adapter, Windows 7 or some combination of them together.

I like that they can be used with a wire as well as with bluetooth. The controls are a little small, as mentioned by others but I don't have trouble working them.

I also tried the JBL EB45T Bluetooth headphones, which cost almost twice as much, at Target and these sound better overall. The JBL might have had better highs, a little punchier bass but these are more cohesive across the frequency range with nothing tweaked to make them sound 'better'.

Summary: I don't have any other Bluetooth headphones to compare these to but I think most people would be very satisfied with these at this price point for general use. If however, you are looking for audiophile on a budget, it's not here.
text_fidelity_b: Jabra Move Style Edition, Black – Wireless Bluetooth Headphones with Superior Sounds Quality, Long Battery Life, Ultra-Light and Comfortable Wireless Headphones, 3.5 mm Jack Connector Included

I tested one out on my husband by placing it at the door he normally enters through. It stopped him, scared him and did just what I hoped it would do. On doors that have windows through which the unwanted guest might peer through and see the doorstop, just by placing a light weight towel or papers over it disguises completely. They'll just think your a slob and leave newspapers on the floor.

My mom was thrilled with her doorstops. Anything to help parents stay safe is money well-spent.

Be aware of how all of your doors open since they won't do any good on doors that open to the outside. The 9 volt battery was a tad difficult to install but I'm not complaining. For my mom I had to write in big letters with a felt permanent marker ON and OFF so she could easily turn them off when not in use and not waste batteries or scare her by an accidental alarm. We'll be taking some of these with us on vacation. These are really great!

UPDATE: December 1, 2011 - I have bought several more of these because they are so practical and good at what they do. I've learned to pick them up by holding the sides of them lest I accidentally hit the metal plate on top and hear it's ear-breaking scream. text_fidelity_a:
Fire Kids Edition Tablet, 7" Display, 8 GB, Blue Kid-Proof Case (Previous Generation - 5th) Very disappointed in Amazon. They ALMOST Got it right. Returned this one quickly.

Let me be clear I am an Amazon Fangirl. I have consistently tried their new things, I have subscribed to prime for years, I love amazon. I love their kindles. So I don't often speak ill of my precious amazon.

I wanted to upgrade my son's kindle ( First gen Fire HD7 ) it's charging port is a bit wobbly and damaged, we've used it for many years and it's got a little wear. That said, it works BETTER Than the current kindle fire. The only problem is you can't play all the same games that I can play on my other kindle and you can't on the new one either. It wants the "NEW HD" ( or my HDX) to play certain games.

Where to begin....first of all the new OS Sucks. It just does. so bad. I'm not even going to rant on that because it's user preference but I found the old OS to be more user friendly and responsive. I have an HDX and it's by far the top notch of them all. I hope I don't have to "upgrade" to this OS.

Storage & Offline use:
You only have 8gb of storage, which wouldn't be an issue thanks to the upgradable microsd slot.. ( GOOD CALL AMAZON) ..EXCEPT They crippled the functionality. For example, I go to the grocery store or road tip with my kid and I let him watch or play on his kindle without being on wifi, you can't do that anymore. Your kids can NOT Watch movies that are downloaded to the microsd card when you are offline. You can't. Not allowed. You can't operate much of anything in the kids profile if you are not connected to wifi. Having 128bg SD card is USELESS for your kids when offline.
I've bought loads of disney movies and the digital copies are all on Amazon for the very reason that they were great to download to our other kindles and watch when we were in the car, plane, or costco.

It won't even let you START The kids freetime profile if you are offline. This severely cripples the device for no good reason. Games and movies which are downloaded to the device or the SD card should work offline in most cases. I've done it on my HDX and my first gen hd. Works just fine in freetime on older devices. No reason for this. And before someone tells me that's what you expect when you stream...I'm not talking about streaming or using netflix, I'm talking about content downloaded to the device. Irrationally Amazon decided that if you are not online, you can go kick rocks.
If you are in an ADULT Profile, I think you can, although I did not try to be fair, because I bought the KIDS Edition for a reason, for my kid to use it.I have my own kindle. No sense in having this for kids if you can't use it when you're out and about. Everyone knows that the screen is the ultimate "quiet time" reward in our parent tool-kit. If you say it's not you're either a liar or an over taxed helicopter parent with way too much techno anxiety. Joking...sorry not sorry.

Kindle FreeTime "unlimited"....
I use the freetime for my son ALL THE TIME. It's amazing, it limits him to what *I* want him to play and watch. I can set a timer for weekends/weekdays that go off at bedtime so that he can "read", watch a show, or play for a short time as a reward before bed. The freetime is
the number one reason I have not gone with an iPad or other device. I can't give my kid any other device with the same level of comfort and control of his screen time and content. I HIGHLY recommend kindles to all my parent friends for this exact reason. It's WELL Worth it. However...it's NOT worth it to use "Unlimited" on this new device. The new kindle sucks for freetime ( See above reason on offline freetime) Mainly tho...it's TERRIBLE for the parent if you've mistakenly turned ON Kindle unlimited. ( If you have an older child, say 9yrs+ this can be mitigated with a nice sit down convo) I'll explain...

Why Freetime Unlimited SUCKS:
I'm speaking of the paid Unlimited service here, the main feature of freetime is still great, with some exceptions ( above) on the new device.

Every single app they touch it will download. If they are curious, and want to see what the game is they instinctively click the app, completely unaware that they have 8gb of space on their tablet and actually it's more like 4gb after the OS. This makes it run Slooooooow and crash. Crash a lot. Crash within the first 60 minutes of your child using the device. Until you go in and fix it, meaning delete them all individually, this device is annoyingly slow and unresponsive. I found out, you can get the apps to download or move them to the memory card, but it will still slow you down once that fills up and you still have to do regular maintaince on the devices memory. The first year of this is free, with this device, but I promise you it's more annoying than worth it. I was an early unlimited subscriber at $2.99 a month and I cancelled it rather quickly, even on my far better HDX and the first gen kindle it was STILL Annoying.

If you have an OLDER Child...this may be mitigated with a sit down conversation as to how their device works, what downloading means, and their storage space. My child is 5, and has proven to not exactly get the concept and download everything willy nilly if given the option.

Do yourself a favor....buy the HD Version, Pray they didn't cripple offline freetime on it, buy the extra warranty and case and and try that instead. That's what I plan to do, I'm going to give it a wait and see if they improve the HD device on the next round. Since the first gen HD 7 still works better than this one, I'll hold out.

Please Amazon....try to get it right next time.
Thanks,
Just another mom.

Datacolor Spyder5EXPRESS – Designed for Hobbyist Photographers (S5X100) I ended up using this colorimeter to profile and calibrate my monitor. Out of the box I was not very happy with the quality of the product. You end up getting pretty much zero instruction and no manual. I had to figure it out on my own just by looking at the product. Once that annoyance was over I got to experience how terrible the default software from datacolor is.

I looked to the reviews and decided I could make the most of this purchase by using other free calibration software. I used Argyll and DispCalGUI. If you simply download DispCalGUI it will prompt you automatically to download the Argyll color libraries.

You then go into Tools->Instrument->install Argyll CMS instrument drivers...

This will download the drivers you need to run the spyder 5.

After this calibration is possible. I calibrated and it seemed to do a decent job. All in all, the calibration software looked like it was powerful--certainly better than the default.

In the end, I returned the product. I wanted something that would work without me having to go the extra mile to get it to work. At this point, with all of the extra I had to do to calibrate I still don't know if it did a good job or not.

Dimensions can be seen in the photos I have attached.

Included is the unit only.

Pros:
*Calibrates
*Decent price

Cons:
*Terrible OEM software (-2 stars)
*Setup--while not hard--is not immediately obvious. A small pamphlet would have gone a long way (-1/2 a star)

Additional Considerations:
Go for hardware that has good software calibration tools. You cant beat the two working in synergy.

Overall: 2.5/5 stars (>=.5 rounds up, <.5 rounds down) => 3 stars

If you have any further questions regarding the product in my review please leave a comment below and I will get back to you as soon as possible.
text_fidelity_b: Datacolor Spyder5EXPRESS – Designed for Hobbyist Photographers (S5X100)

Fire TV Stick with Voice Remote This product has a lot of promise, but fails to deliver in some areas, and is just plan not user friendly in others.
My experience on this product was that it arrived a day late, and when it arrived it would not work with my Visio High Definition Television. The TV either did not recognize it or it did not recognize my TV. So I dragged another High Definition Television into the room that I had (LG) and it immediately began working. Set up was fairly simple, however some of the setup features are where my annoyance began. This device every now and again asks for codes for WiFi and other settings that were already input. Things like Hulu and Netflix ask me every now and again if I want to sign up or login as an existing user. Why does it randomly do this? My Roku remembered me, why cant this. Amazon Prime offers password protection to prevent family members or other unwanted individuals from charging content to your credit card through a six digit pin. However the only way to input that pin (other than downloading an app to your phone) is to use an awkward scroll wheel, and additionally oddly marked buttons to get through the numerous number menu options. It is a bit of a pain. The voice control feature is a waste of money, it only finds items that Amazon can charge you for. I attempted to look up Thomas the Train for my daughter which was not only available free for Prime Members but was also on Netflix and Hulu which I had and was free, instead all it would find was items that Amazon could charge for. This is a common problem with the voice command feature. This when coupled with the horrendous navigation menus and difficulty finding what you want make this a poor choice considering other options from Roku, Apple TV and others. A little more tweaking and this could be a great product.

text_fidelity_a: Beats Studio Wireless Over-Ear Headphone - Matte Black (Old Model) These headphones do have a more balanced sound than the horrible original Beats that were just too bass heavy. The Bluetooth pairing was quick and easy and battery life is decent. The case and accessories seem to be good quality. In all honesty though for the sound quality I'd never pay the retail asking price for these or recommend them to anyone. I got a used pair (yes they are real Beats) for half the price of new and at this price point I feel it's worth it. The noise canceling isn't anything to write home about and if it's a big reason why you're considering these I'd look to Bose or elsewhere where it's done much better. Another point with these is comfort. They're ok for an hour or so, but I'd not want these on pushing two or more. They tend to pinch at the ear cup level and you can see in various pics how the cups nearly touch when not on the head. So the farther you are pushing those cups out the more they are fighting to close so to speak. I don't have a large head, I don't expand the headband at all when wearing, and they get a little clampy after a bit. Another comfort issue is the interior depth of the ear cups. I don't have big ear or ones that stick out and I still feel my ears slightly pushing against the speaker. I couldn't imagine anyone with large ears being happy with these at all and if you fall into that category I'd definitely try on a pair in a store before buying. The cup pads are nice and it's too bad they didn't make them just a tad deeper.  So in summary these are good headphones if not great ones, but honestly not worth retail. The Bluetooth is nice, but you're obviously paying for image here.

text_fidelity_a:
Cooler Master Hyper 212 EVO V2 CPU Air Cooler with SickleFlow 120, PWM Fan, Direct Contact Technology, 4 Copper Heat Pipes for AMD Ryzen/Intel LGA1700/1200/1151, Silver/Black I have had this CPU fan now going on 5 months. I love this fan. I hadn't upgraded for nearly 10 years and decided on an AMD FM2 Black Edition 6300 6-core CPU with an MSI 970A-G43 Plus economy Micro Board and 16GB of Corsair Memory 4GBx4 in the 4 slots. I use my computer for gaming and all around use. I wanted a CPU cooler that would be quiet and still keep my cpu cool when I cranked it up for high-performance gaming. I found it with this AND it didn't break the bank. With the Turbo Clock OC setting it will idle down and bolt up to 4300mhz seamlessly while the fan moves from it's WHISPER silent 36c idle and general use, to it's 42c full bore o'clocked gaming use. The fan keeps it cool, and never does the fan become obtrusive or loud.

This fan is BIG. Don't even consider it if you have a micro or small mid-tower case. Your case must be generous in it's width to accommodate this cooler. Be sure to check the dimensions of your case with the unit. I have an older Antec 900 case it fit snugly into. I did have to remove the optional side window cooler intake fan I had installed with the prev board, cpu and cooler to allow it's fit. Also be sure your motherboard design placement of Memory slots is such that your Memory will clear it. My board's Corsair Vengence Memory JUST cleared it by a couple mm's laterally, and the top of the memory overtakes the bottom edge of cooler by about a quarter inch. If you are in the process of building your system a choice with low profile memory that doesn't have the tall heat spreaders would be a wise choice and safe bet if you are unsure about clearance with a board design that puts the memory slots very close to the CPU and cooler position. In the first photo attached I REVERSED the fan position to PULL the air thru on Left for best clearance instead of PUSHING the air through on the right if you just don't have the room, that flexibility is very handy. I wasn't satisfied with the cooling level and re-positioned the fan on right to PUSH it through later on and it sent the temps down a few more degrees. As you can see though in the second photo, it is much more snug.

Bottom line, a great cooler IF your case and build offers the room to fit it in. I would recommend it for those wanting great overclocking cooling performance and very quiet operation. I think most overclock enthusiasts would be well served to try this value priced solution before expensive and complicated water cooled solutions.
text_fidelity_b: Cooler Master Hyper 212 EVO V2 CPU Air Cooler with SickleFlow 120, PWM Fan, Direct Contact Technology, 4 Copper Heat Pipes for AMD Ryzen/Intel LGA1700/1200/1151, Silver/Black

text_fidelity_a:
ZOMEi Tripod, 65" Camera Tripod for Canon Nikon DSLR, Aluminum Alloy Tripod with 360 Degree Ball Head, Professional Tripod for Travel and Work (Orange) This tripod is advertised as 65 inches tall, but that is misleading since you can only reach that height with the center post full extended and somewhat unstable. Most tripods are measured with just the legs and not including the center post or head. This one is about 50 inches tall or 57 inches with the included ball head. You can compare that measurement to other brands.

For a tripod of this height, this one is relatively lightweight and folds up into a compact 20-inch-long case. That makes it very portable for field use. However, they did have to make a lot of compromises in stability to make it this compact and lightweight. The legs have 4 sections (compared to 2 or 3 sections on sturdier tripods) and the thinnest sections are somewhat flexy under moderate weight or in a moderate wind. I don't trust this tripod with a mid-weight SLR camera and exposures of more than 1 second (unless you have the legs folded to half length). For a lightweight camera and fast exposure, this tripod is fine. However, I still would not trust extending the center post in windy conditions, since that amplifies the instability of the tripod legs.

The tripod is attractively finished. I do not like all the twist locks that are slow to operate (compared to cam-locks) and with 4 leg sections, this tripod has lots of twist-locks.

The ball head works OK for this price level and has a quick release plate that also works OK. This company has several different quick release plates sold separately, hopefully one of those will work with this tripod so you can easily use different cameras on it. I have not tried to figure out which one to buy yet, though.

Other people are complaining about the zipper on the case. The zipper on my case broke on the first day of use, too. Just the zipper pull, which is not too expensive to replace.

In summary, this tripod works OK for this price level if you are using a smaller camera and fast exposures. If their goal was to make a lightweight portable tripod, I wish they had made it sturdier and shorter instead of flimsy and taller.
text_fidelity_b: ZOMEi Tripod, 65" Camera Tripod for Canon Nikon DSLR, Aluminum Alloy Tripod with 360 Degree Ball Head, Professional Tripod for Travel and Work (Orange)

text_fidelity_a:
myCharge PowerGear Sound Protective Portable Charging Case for Wireless Earbuds Headphones | Custom Tray Compatible with Powerbeats & Removable for Other Brands | 1400 mAh / 1A Output The MyCharge is a handy if not tiny clamshell charging case for PowerBeat headphones, though it will work for others as well.

Pros:
The case itself has an hard outer shell that feels durable and thick. I have no fears the earbuds will be well protected inside. It opens and closes easily and tightly. As much as a case can be, it’s aesthetically pleasing—a dark, slick black with a black ribbon with red stitching running down the middle (the red stitching matches the red inside). The ribbon/band does more than add a bit of style and color; it also gives it a bit more texture so it grips the surface it’s atop better.

The plastic tray inside is designed for the PoweBeats line, so the earbuds nestle snugly (but with no need to wrestle or force them in) into an indentation so they lie flat and with a mid-section to insert the connecting wires/controls into. It’s a good fit, well-designed, and I don’t feel like I’m overstressing the wires, though I wouldn’t want to leave them in that position for a long amount of time (though I tend to worry about that sort of thin more than others)

It comes with a cable. You can use any one, but you’ll want it to be very short

The port to charge the case (the battery inside the case for sticklers) is easily accessible.

An LED on the front lets you know if the case battery is getting low

Cons
I wish the port cover felt a little more durable

Mixed or Up in the Air
I haven’t had it long enough yet to check how many charges, but I’ve gotten a few without a noticeable impact on the case battery. I don’t know if their promise of a dozen-plus will bear out, but I don’t think it’ll be far off if not.

The case isn’t really tiny (You can see the dimensions above). If you’re looking for something to slip into a pocket, then this will be a con, though it will easily fit a coat pocket. It will fit cargo pockets but you’ll definitely know it’s there. On the other hand, it doesn’t take up a lot of space, it’s quite protective, and if you’re worried about losing your expensive but very small and easy to lose earbuds, putting them in a noticeable, protective case that will also charge them back up is far from the worst idea. Personally, I’m OK with the size.

As noted, the case is designed for PowerBeats, so your mileage will vary on how well it fits some other type. My other earbuds all fits in the case without an issue, just not as snugly or neatly. That isn’t a real priority for me even ignoring the fact that I have PowerBeats.

Overall, a good value for what it does I’d say.
